8762:
The unit only overrides the Cartridge slot and displays status.
It should keep running with NO controllers plugged in, as it is
testing the Arcade hardware only and assumes the handles are off.

Trouble with using MESS is the knob is simulated by Z & X keys
and only if you slow the rate down can you get it to $00 or $FF.

NOP'ed out this test at $235C so it runs without a Knob Error :

        JR     NZ,A23CF         ; Error 14

Then found out it does a checksum on ITSELF, so I had to change
its check-sum byte to $C8 so it would pass and get beyond that.

Now it does just four passes then loops waiting for key entries
showing only the byte mid-scren it used for Shift/Flop/etc tests
(first pass might be black-on-black, give it a few seconds) :

A23BD   JR     A23BD    ; Loop forever, but process interrupts

where you can enter keypad commands using this key translation :

MESS = pad - Command (comment)

 C = 1 - Memory Read (4-Hex digits Address, loops reading)
Up = 2 - Memory Write (2-digit Data, 4-digit Address, loops)
Dn = 3 - Input Port Read (2-digit Port number, loops reading)
 O = 4 - Output Port Write (2-digit Data, 2-digit Port, loops)
 R = 5 - Memory Read and Write (2-digit Data, 4-digit Address)
 S = 6 - Display all Input Devices (Crashes in MESS 0.126 ?)
 H = 7 - Rainbow Color Display (almost as nice as RAINBOW v3)
kp/ = 8 - Enter Machine Code From Keypad (see * note below)
 7 = 9
 8 = A
 9 = B
kp* = C
 4 = D
 5 = E
 6 = F
kp- = 0
 1 = Q/S (select Burn-in mode or 4-pass Bench mode)
 E = CE (Clear Entry - unless already looping)
kpEnter = Go (Run, but crashes on bad code!)
and ...
F3 or <Options | Soft Reset> = RESET button (only way to restart)

Once it starts one of the routines it keeps looping that function
so the repairman can hook up an oscilloscope and see what's what.

Holding the Q/S key (Quit/Stop ??) at the right time will make it
loop the tests forever - but it is also supposed to bail out ??/?

* note: when entering machine code 4444 is a nice place to start.
Clear Entry only erases the first digit of the byte, be careful.

Happy Bal-Checking!! Have up-loaded it as X_BALCHK.bin - save to:
MESS/software/astrocdw/ for WHITE.ROM - WON'T work for Astrocades.

Remember to lower your sound, it almost as bad as Muncher's noise.

Richard Degler

8763:
I added several files so that the Astrocade can be emulated via hardware.  The Astrocade can be emulated in hardware because of Mike J's hard work recreating the console (in low-res AND hi-res mode) for an FPGA chip in the hardware descriptor language VHDL.  This version will run on a Xilinx Spartan3E starter kit board, but it may be able to be ported to other boards.

This is a pretty complicated subject that most people won't be able to try because you need special hardware.  However, for an overview, here is some information from Mike J's FAQ:

"Very simply, VHDL is a high level language which is used to design and simulate hardware, by which I mean everything from a modern complex CPU to a digital watch.  Software tools take the VHDL source code, and hopefully convert it into real physical logic gates.  This can then (at vast expense) be turned into a piece of silicon and sold to people.  I should point out that only a subset of the language can actually be turned into gates, as some constructs are only useful for simulating designs."

"VHDL stands for VHSIC Hardware Description Language, where VHSIC is an acronym for Very High Speed Integrated Circuit.  However, the name is more frightening than the language, which resulted from a US Government sponsored effort to improve the way integrated circuit designs were exchanged between companies.  The IEEE adopted VHDL as a standard in 1987 (1076-1987)."

You can visit the Astrocade Hardware Emulation Area here:

http://tinyurl.com/create.php

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/emulation/hardware_emulation/hardware_emulation.html

For more information visit Mike J's Bally FPGA Arcade page at:

http://www.fpgaarcade.com/bally_main.htm

Have fun!

Adam

8767:
In whaever BalCheck you're using (what's the name of the binary
conditionally assembled as NEWROM, modified for the Astrocades?)
hope you made an overlay for it.  Here's how to play Gunfight...

Create a stub that will CALL MACTINT then JP GFSTRT using '8'
then "4444" and enter "CD","8B","01","C3","DE","17" then 'GO'.

Those routines are in the same place throughout all three bios,
and the other on-board games should work, replacing after "C3":
"28","13" for CMSTRT (CheckMate)
"20","10" for CALCST (Calculator)
"19","0E" for SCBST (Scribbling)

but ...
For MESS that's "/","OOOO","*4","/9","-C","*v","45","CH" where
those are letter 'O's, numbers are in the top row, arithmetic
symbols are from the keypad ONLY and 'v' is the Page Down key.

Run with 'keypadEnter' - and for the others replace after "*v":
"^/","Cv" for CMSTRT (CheckMate)
"^-","C-" for CALCST (Calculator)
"C7","-5" for SCBST (Scribbling)
What key does the '^' stand for?  You got it, the Page Up key!

That's a lot of work when you could have pressed RESET instead,
plus you have to guess at what the Options menu is asking for.

Just don't say it can't be done -
Richard

Has anyone encounter anything like this before?

Some clean-up that I do after running dZ80 2.0 (with built-in LUA
support) is to capitalize the first 6 characters in every line since
even with upper-case selected the labels are in lower-case.  Use a
suitable text editor (or maybe a DOS batch file could do it.)
Quite a few commands have un-needed spaces trailing them.  Delete those
if your editor can do it all-at-once.

There's a switch to insert a blank line after each RETurn found, but it
also puts one after conditional RETs which I don't like.  Since
non-conditional jumps also should mark a break in program flow I search
for "JP      L" or "JR      L" as well as "RET"s with a macro to insert
a CR and Search, or Search again to skip.  Less used is "JP      (HL)"
so I do those as I come across them.

Unfortunately, when my script puts a semi-colon to mark the end of a UPI
(User Program Interface) Macro it duplicates the Label if there is one
on the next line.  Have to clean those up by hand.

It also lines up the comments over with the Jump Relative offsets. I
always move them in closer by Replacing All "eight-spaces, semi-colon,
two-spaces" with just "semi-colon, one-space".
This is why there are two spaces before the comments!  Not really, but I
left the extra one in since it came in handy for this!!



Use a mono-spaced font to view the output.  Courier New is a standard
one.
Don't use any TABs because what lines up for you might not for others.
Is that six or eight spaces?  Full count or in columns from the left
edge??

That seems like a lot of extra steps, but it's better than working from
scratch.

Richard C Degler

As far as I know, there are 3 ways for code to become a assembled program. Richard, please correct me if I'm wrong.

1) Hand assembly. This is how I learned machine language. I took a BASIC "word processor" that was written by Don Gladden and changed it into 95% machine language. The other 5% are all input /output commands that I didn't have any knowledge of how they were done and where they were in BRB 1.1. If I remember right it only had about 5 lines in BASIC. Most were OP commands.

2) Use an assembler. These take the code you have written, no matter what "holes" are in it, and puts the "tags' together. (A label and it's subroutine)

3) a compiler. These, if done right, have "smarts" about them. They try to put code into some sort of order. If you have a GOOD compiler, it will find such things as once called routines and put them in line without the call and return. These were extremely rare and VERY expensive during the Bally years.
Ken

Sounds good to me.  Hand coding is how I wrote all my Bally stuff.

An ASSEMBLER replaces OpCodes in a source file with machine code.
Routines can be placed at any memory address with an ORG statement
or alternatively, padding NUL bytes can be added to position them.
Source code can be all in one file or INCLUDE'd as separate files.

Used a cross-assembler (non-native) to finish my "Conway's Life".
It was also called a two-pass assembler - first identifies Labels
in the source and then goes through again using that infomation.
(Video Storybook appears to have been assembled in only one pass!)

It can also be a macro-assembler if there is a pre-processor pass
which expands macros (naturally) and does conditional assembling.

And ...
Basic on the Bally/Astrocade is INTERPRETED on the fly.  Keywords
are listed in a program and it takes extra time to translate them.
(Coloring Book was a FORTH program with an Interpreter to run it!!)

But ...
A COMPILER recognizes only "Higher Level" language such as C, C++
or even Basic and turns words like IF and THEN into a lot of code.


Richard

I have added Barry McCleave's "Fawn Dungeon" (AKA: D&D For Bally) source code in ready-to-assemble format.  This code was written by Barry in 1981.  I have retyped and disassembled it over the last few days so that it can be assembled using ZMac.

For those not already aware, this is an incomplete machine language game.  The player in this D&D-type game can wander around a maze, but there are no monsters or objects to interact with.  This is an interesting piece of what might have become something interesting.  As it stands, it is little more than a programming exercise.  As Ken Lill writes in his newest version of the UltiMulti Cartridge, "This is a program that was started by Barry McCleave who has since passed on.  This can be used to see how to move something in machine language.  Want to finish it?"

Notes about this version:

1) Changed source code from 8080 to Z80 machine language.

2) Final output matches EXACTLY with the binary version that works correctly.

3) Although this version DOES match 100% with the working ROM image, it does so at the expense of not using labels for the new areas that were added.  Those areas are HARD CODED.  If any code is added to the source code, without adding labels, then the binary will not work correctly. 

You can download the source code here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/ml/ml_source/Fawn_Dungeon_Assembly_Listing.z80

While typing in the source, I have discovered some interesting information.  There is much more to this game then meets the eye.  For instance, I thought that the Cowboy graphic was called from the ROM to save cartridge ROM space.  But no, it wasn't.  It was copied and is actually part of the source code.  So, if anybody with some artistic talent wants to create a knight or someone in armor... then have at it!

I'm going to compile a text document that covers some of my discoveries and share it with everyone in the next few days.

I know that there are not a lot of assembly-writing folks on this board, but if anyone has any comments...

Enjoy!

Adam

8840:
After looking at the program, I know it would be easier to do this into any extended memory unit. !6000 can be accessed by all BASICS and is a good place to store things instead of @(n) strings. The main problem with poking into these addresses is that it uses up 4 more byte in the basic program per each address addressed, if the @(n) number is is less than 10. The way around that is to use a variable for the address number. Then just say %(A) =, and then increment A as necessary.
!6000 is 6000 hex or 24576 decimal, which is what the 2 different Bally BASICs use. Then when you want to store this, just do a :PRINT ; :PRINT %(24576),bytes divided by 2+RM. To get it back use :INPUT ;:INPUT %(25676) ;RUN
Ken

8851:
I'm delving into some more of Bob Fabris' recorded conversations, and one piece of history that I hadn't heard about is the attempted aquisition of Bally's computer division by Fidelity Electronics in 1980.  There's a brief mention of it in this article:

http://www.ballyalley.com/articles_and_news/creative_computing_article.pdf

Apparently, it got scuttled because the distributors were afraid of getting shut out.  The phone calls make clear that the deal was very close to going through, with Fidelity giving a letter of intent to Bally, and Bally announcing the plans.  It also seems that a lot of people were excited about the deal, as Fidelity had a good reputation.

The recordings include Bob Fabris calling Ron Nelson.  Ron is known for helping to create the first commercial electronic chess machine, Fidelity Chess Challenger I, in 1977.  Here's some more information about him and the company:

http://www.ismenio.com/fidelity.html

http://www.spacious-mind.com/html/fidelity.html

http://www.computerhistory.org/chess/main.php?sec=thm-42f15c9b2be73&sel=thm-42f15cb7b49f0

No doubt in some parallel universe, Fidelity brought the Fidelity Professional Arcade to the front of the videogame pack, prevented the videogame crash of 1982, and is now developing the Fidelity Arcade 2010 that interfaces directly with your brain.

Paul

8855:
As I was hoping, the Bob Fabris audio recordings are becoming more clear as I listen to more of them.  For one thing, I can now recognize Jeff Frederiksen's voice.  I also know that Ed Larkin was a major force behind Alternative Engineering's attempt to release a ZGRASS expansion.  So, here are some updated descriptions for many of the recordings already on-line.


12-17_Fenton

Bob calls Jay Fenton. They largely discuss plans for a system add-under, and speculate about many interesting features it could have. At this point, it's planned to be 60K RAM and ROM. Bob's also been talking to Jeff Frederiksen about it. Jay mentions some of the software he's working on, including Extended BASIC, The Game Of Life, and Morse code software. They also lament how the system, despite being very powerful, isn't selling that well and is apt to break. Jay was once roommates with Dick Ainsworth, but now Dick's fallen in love, and has moved in with his girlfriend and is converting to vegetarianism.


Larkin_1-28_(part_1)

Bob Fabris calls Ed Larkin of Alternative Engineering and arranges to get Muncher carts manufactured. Bob's going to be taking orders for them, which would make the year 1983. Also, Alternative Engineering is gearing up for a small initial run of ZGRASS expansions. Esoterica is involved, but Dan Dresher wants to keep it secret. They're having trouble raising the capital to get started.


Larkin_1-28_(part_2)

Bob Fabris talks to Ed Larkin again. ZGRASS expansion development is running into problems. They've had to switch to an external power supply so they'll have enough power to run later additions like a disk drive. They've also switched from a plastic to a metal case, both to get FCC approval and because it looks better. They're even offering a metal case to put the Bally system in, and plan to sell some complete systems since a dealer is dumping Ballys for $50 apiece. The expansion will cost $2000. A high-res board is coming out later. The recording ends suddenly as the tape runs out.


Larkin_1-28_(reverse)

Bob Fabris talks to Ed Larkin about ZGRASS some more (maybe the same conversation as that in "Larkin_1-28_(part_2).wav" . It will be compatible with the cartridge slot, and can work with a light pen and, in theory, could be expanded to use laserdiscs. Esoterica hasn't seen the new case yet, and they're planning to surprise them with it. Bob asks about getting discounted units for programmers. It's now almost September, and they want to get it out by Christmas. He says they're ready to rip off their arms and legs to get it released. They're ready to start taking orders, but are displeased with ABC Hobbycraft for advertising it and asking for immediate payment.


TEL. CONVERSATIONS Copy 11-28

Bob Fabris asks Jeff Frederiksen about possible new features for the ZGRASS add-under. These include an S-100 adapter card (to allow different peripherals to plug in), scientific calculations (already being worked on), and a ROM burner (S-100 could help you hook one up). They also discuss using Bally BASIC to save data files, and using a printer with BASIC. They arrange to meet later to discuss further details. Bob will be in Washington on, he believes, Tuesday Dec. 11, 1979.

Paul
8856:
Here are my notes on the next set of recordings--hosted by Bob Fabris, with an all-star cast featuring Jeff Frederiksen, Tom Meeks, Ed Larkin, Tom DeFanti, and Jane Veeder.  Don't miss special guest star Ron Nelson, and keep your ears open for a cameo appearance by Ray George!

Question of the day--where is Ed Larkin?  This guy sounds like the real driving force behind the final attempt to release a ZGRASS expansion.  If anyone has a few prototypes sitting in his basement, it would be him.


Meeks_2-1-83_part_1.flac -- Bob Fabris talks to Tom Meeks.  Tom discusses an attempt to release the Astrocade in Europe.  They've gotten a sample to a company called ITT, and everyone is optimistic.  Ray George is really pushing to get ZGRASS out this year.  Bally itself is also pushing both these ventures, and may even provide financial backing for ZGRASS.  No new consoles are being manufactured at the moment, though there is still old stock to sell.  Astrocade is in some sort of dispute with Nitron.  Bob says there's been a good response to the ad in Electronic Games.  Arcadian subscribers are stable at about 2,000.  Tom doesn't think the BASIC manual did a good job of getting people into programming.  Tom's going to get Bob mailing addresses from warranty cards.  Astrocade's getting ready to go do court over debts.  Creditors are going after money Astrocade's gotten from Montgomery Ward--money they need to keep the company running.  Tom's trying to arrange to leave Astrocade with a severance package, but wants to keep consulting with them on ZGRASS.  Tom's been doing lots of ZGRASS programming, developing educational children's programs.  He gives some details about ZGRASS programming, strengths, and limitations.

Meeks_2-1-83_part_2.flac -- Bob Fabris talks to Ed Larkin of Alternative Engineering.  They discuss the Electronic Games "underground" article.  He's manufacturing Pac-Man carts for Bob.  They joke about the secrecy around it.  He's developing a communication board.  The company doesn't have a lot of capital to work with.

Meeks_2-1-83_(reverse)_part_1.flac -- Bob Fabris talks to Tom Meeks.  Astrocade has entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy.  Nitron's stock has suspended trading for two days, and Tom expects Nitron to fail.  In Tom's view, this situation is partly Nitron's fault, because he believes they were trying to take control of Astrocade from the day they started building the systems.  He places more blame on Astrocade, however.  Tom hopes ITT can rejuvenate the system by building it cheaper than they can.  Tom thinks the bankruptcy will help them get a little sympathy and curiosity at the upcoming CES show.  They haven't been able to implement anything lately, even though they're getting lots of good suggestions, particularly from Dan Houser.  Astrocade has at least been getting more free publicity lately.

Meeks_2-1-83_(reverse)_part_2.flac -- Bob Fabris talks to Bob (Ogden?).  With Astrocade in the midst of bankruptcy, Bob (Ogden?) is looking into releasing future games through U.S. Games.  There's still hope of rescue from ITT, though.  Bob Fabris wants to put together an independent advisory panel to guide software development.  One interested party is Alternative Engineering.  With Astrocade not making games at the moment, Bob (Ogden?) isn't particularly interested in this for now.

Meeks_2-1-83_(reverse)_part_3.flac -- Bob Fabris talks to Ed Larkin about three weeks after the Astrocade bankruptcy.  According to Ed, Bob Ogden expects to have a deal with ITT within the next couple of weeks.  At this point, Ed will start working for Bob Ogden to help address the lack of software for the system.  Ed sees ITT as a much more professional company than Astrocade, and hopes they take over the whole business.  Bob Fabris suggests he consider producing ZGRASS for them rather than for Astrocade, and gives out contact information for Nicholas Gibbs at ITT Consumer Products (UK) Limited.  Ed talked to Tom Meeks just before the bankruptcy for a little help with ZGRASS, but couldn't get much support.  This may have been related to the stress of the impending bankruptcy and Tom looking for a different job.  ITT is hoping to make the hardware compatible with both the US and Europe, and to re-release it in the US at a lower cost.  Right now, Astrocade could only bring in operating capital with new products.  They haven't paid John Perkins for work on a game, so he's planning to release the game through another company.  Bob talks to Ed about manufacturing Pac-Man carts, and wants to change the name to Munch Kid.  They're going to make 100 carts, with Bob putting up about $1,000 upfront and $1,000 on delivery.  The recording ends suddenly.

Sales_Pitch_for_New_BASIC_Bally_ARCADE_+.flac -- This seems to be a presentation for the Astrocade marketing team.  The first speaker is Jeff Frederiksen.  He thinks there's a big demand for fantasy games, and there are no good computer fantasy games on the market.  So, they're about to release Wizard of Wor.  He says Astrocade is better than Bally at marketing.  A next generation system, with new custom chips, is already being designed.  He compares Astrocade technology to Atari.  The next generation system will be able to display 16 colors out of a palette of over two million.  He expects it to be way ahead of the competition.  He says Bally BASIC was made to show that the system was a real computer.  One reason BASIC wasn't more successful is that it required too much investment--a system, cart, and interface.  So now, they've got a new BASIC with a faster, built-in interface.  And the cart is going to be packed in with the system.  Ray George interjects that it will now be called the Bally Arcade Plus.  Jeff demonstrates loading a BASIC program.  He says Bally BASIC has the advantage of simple graphics programming.  The tape ends with a question and answer session.  Jeff doesn't think voice synthesis is worth pursuing this generation.  The recording ends when they take a coffee break.

Sales_Pitch_for_New_BASIC_Bally_ARCADE_+_(reverse).flac -- The meeting continues with Jeff talking about the add-under.  It will include a modem, parallel port, and floppy drive.  He discusses the memory in the add-under.  Bally is investing money in the add-under, even though it will be released by Astrovision.  He talks about the size of the games industry.  Next, Tom DeFanti shows a high-resolution ZGRASS demo by Jane Veeder.  Tom says it's important that the add-under will put out a video signal that can be recorded and televised.  Jane herself begins speaking.  She shows the Montana demo.  Tom starts speaking again.  He wants to make the machine accessible such that, for example, an accountant could write an accountant program.  Parents could even write programs instead of bed-time stories.  Someone asks how he can convince someone that the machine with the add-under will bring money into their organization.  Tom responds that by including a high level language, third parties will be able to create software much more easily.  Jeff adds that graphic creation is very easy.  Tom says that ultimately, it will be sold by showing it rather than talking about it.  Initially, he expects the add-under to sell to people who want to move up from Bally BASIC.  Then, as people see other people using it, and as more software becomes available, it will become more popular.  Jeff and Tom prepare another demonstration.  Jeff explains that Tom has been working for months to improve ZGRASS, so it will be even better than what they're demonstrating.  Tom and Jeff discuss some of the advantages of ZGRASS over BASIC.  Showing the color capabilities leads to a brief discussion from the audience about Color BASIC.  The recording ends while they're demonstrating ZGRASS commands.

7_call_JF.flac -- After a date declaration of June 26 (1980), Bob Fabris calls Jeff Frederiksen.  Bob has been talking to Jay Fenton about his development of an extended BASIC cartridge, and Bob's put him in touch with third parties developing RAM expansions.  Bob asks if Bally will be selling the extended BASIC cartridge directly, and Jeff says the plan is to sell it as a limited edition at probably about $75.  [This is mentioned in Arcadian volume 2, issue 9, page 78.]  They discuss advertising for it in the Sourcebook.  It will search for any contiguous RAM block above the screen RAM.  They're planning on making a commercial ZGRASS system package at a cost of about $3000 (with about $700 of that for the monitor).  It's not being aimed at amateurs.  They're planning to demonstrate it at SIGGRAPH next month.  The recording ends suddenly.

7_call_JF_(reverse)_part_1.flac -- Bob Fabris and Jeff Frederiksen talk about the ZGRASS expansion--possibly the same conversation as on the front side of the tape.  Jeff mentions a module for voice synthesis and light pen for graphics editing.  It can either stand alone or act as a slave to another computer system.  He says there will be applications for it when it's released.

7_call_JF_(reverse)_part_2.flac -- Bob Fabris talks to Jeff Frederiksen.  Bob asks about cartridge parts, since some people want to manufacture their own Videocades.  Jeff says they're custom made, but they'd be willing to sell EEPROM carts to people.  They discuss the sound registers, and Bob compliments Brett Bilbrey's sound work.  Bob mentions work on a keyboard addition, and asks about ASCII codes for commands.  There are rumors about the system being taken over from Bally by another company, but Jeff doesn't have any news about it.  Jeff demonstrates Vortrax speech synthesis.  Jeff's found a modification to the audio interface that makes it more reliable.  [This is detailed in Arcadian volume 2, issue 8, page 71.]

Bally_Larkin_Conversation.flac -- Ed Larkin reads an advertisement for the Viper System 1 to Bob Fabris.

Nelson_2-1_80.flac -- Bob Fabris calls Ron Nelson of Fidelity Electronics.  Bob asks about recent developments, and Ron says that the current situation is that Bally is pushing to quickly divest from the system, but Fidelity wants to slow down and look over the contract closely.  Bob also mentions the development of a hobbyist memory addition and keyboard.  It's planned to be sold as a kit, in part to avoid the need for FCC approval.

Leske_Freeman_1-8_part_1.flac -- Bob Fabris talks to Larry Leske, who's been working on a programmable keyboard kit. [Arcadian volume 1, issue 8, page 55]  It seems likely that Fidelity Electronics will take over the system, and they plan on possibly reviving the ZGRASS add-under in about six months.  Larry has great respect for the engineering at Fidelity, and thinks it's likely they'll get out a quality product fairly quickly.  Given this, Larry doesn't really want to compete with them, so the project is put on hold.  [Arcadian volume 2, issue 3, page 19]

Leske_Freeman_1-8_part_2.flac -- Bob Fabris talks to Bob Freeman, who's been working on an S-100 adapter for the sysetem [Arcadian volume 2, issue 2, page 11].  With Larry Leske losing interest on programmable keyboard work, Fabris is now particularly interested in this.  Freeman is also thinking about things like a modem.  But he's not moving at a fast pace unless there's enough interest to make it profitable.  Fabris is planning on surveying the Arcadian readers on what they want.  [Arcadian volume 2, issue 3, page 19].  Freeman has also programmed a system monitor ROM, to be used for debugging assembler programs.  Freeman wonders if Fidelity Electronics would consider speeding up the system's Z80, but Fabris says they're trying to cut costs on the board instead.  They might consider a retrofit kit, though.

they're getting lots of good suggestions, particularly from Dan Houser.

Astrocade has at least been getting more free publicity lately.

Yea... but mostly negative.

looking into releasing future games through U.S. Games.

Why the Hell does Muncher have so many different names?!?

They're going to make 100 [Muncher] carts

I wonder if that's the final count for the carts made by Bob?

With all of the people at this sales pitch... I would have LOVED to have been there!  Wow!

A next generation system, with new custom chips, is already being designed.

What?!?  This is the first that I've heard of it!

>>
The next generation system will be able to display 16 colors out of a palette of over two million.

Two million color palette?!?  Let me get this straight.  Only 4-bit color able to be displayed onscreen, but out of an approximate

Bally is investing money in the add-under, even though it will be released by Astrovision.

Why would they do that?

>>
Tom DeFanti shows a high-resolution ZGRASS demo by Jane Veeder.
>>

I wonder if Jane has video tape of this sort of thing?

>>
Tom says it's important that the add-under will put out a video signal that can be recorded and televised.
>>

In a way, this is what happened with the Amiga.  Since the video was standard NTSC or PAL, the Video Toaster was invented.  For many people the Amiga computer wasn't even a computer at all... it was a Video Toaster.  That seems to be kind of what the UV-1 was.  Well, KINDA.

>>
Jane herself begins speaking. She shows the Montana demo.

We do have a picture of this:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/misc/Montana-Jane_Veeder.jpg

>>
[Tom] wants [it so that] Parents could even write programs instead of bed-time stories.

Tom mentions this in one of the videos that Paul pointed out some time back.  I thought that this was an unusual statement at the time and I think it is even more so now.  I have a son who is sixteen and when he was younger (at the age when you read "bed-time stories") I would NEVER have supplemented that with cool programs that I wrote.  The idea of bed-time stories isn't the reading of them, nor is it the idea of hearing them.  The purpose is to bond with your child.  That's not going to happen through a computer.

Jeff explains that Tom has been working for months to improve ZGRASS

I didn't realize that Tom was a programmer working on Z-GRASS at all.

This would be the UV-1, which WAS released.  The audience, as stated, WAS limited and thus the release was quite limited as well.  The final price was WAY off though.  The basic UV-1 unit (WITHOUT monitor) cost $7,695 in January of 1983.  That's not even including everything that's actually needed to operate it.  The total cost for a basic unit, with everything needed to use it, was $12,039.  FAR, FAR out of an "amateur" user's range for SURE!  You can view the January 1983 price listing here:

If this actually happened, then this is recorded on Video, as were all of the SIGGRAPH meetings.  Some years back I saw that these could still be ordered.  This should probably be investigated.

On the Bally?  I used to have a Vortex speech synthesizer that connected to serial ports.  It could be used on most home computers because of this (thought they usually needed an adapter).  I wish that I still have this hardware.

hobbyist memory addition and keyboard [..] planned to be sold as a kit, in part to avoid the need for FCC approval.

Great stuff, Paul!

8861:
This brings back SO MANY MEMORIES.

I worked with ITT on later digital TV chips with Frederiksen.

And yes, there was a 4 bit - 16 color - system that we were working on.
The color display worked by Indexed lookup. In memory there is a pixel defined by 4 bits. Those 4 bits point to one of 16 registers that have a 24 bit lookup. I actually think it would have been a 24 bit lookup, and that for the 2 million colors someone just screwed up counting in binary... ;-)

This is the same way the Arcade works, but with 2 bits in memory pointing to 24 bit registers.

Brett

8866:
You have to remember that this was Bally.
They kept on going and built the next generation game platform, then the next, and the next...
Some platforms were built by DNA, some by Midway.
Midway made a pretty good system that was used for a few games, the "Jupiter/Saturn/Neptune" development systems. For a while they were named after planets...

And to your other question, about the relationship between Bally and Astrocade.
Bally wanted to go forward and build video games for commercial use, but have a partner established in the consumer market that could focus on and sell into that consumer market. If things had gone well, then Astrocade might have had future game systems based on later Bally chips. But none of that happened. So it is a moot point...

I'm glad that you are going through these tapes!  To me, these audio recordings are as important as archiving the Astrocade software (maybe even MORE so).  Certainly, I think that more people can relate to these recordings than to most of the BASIC software.  Unless people have used BASIC before on SOME computer, then it's hard to imagine using BASIC programs on ANY computer, let alone the Astrocade.  It's rather easy for people to listen to a recording and "get it."  Not only are the audio recordings of historical value, but they kinda make you fell like you are there, at the very moment when the discussion is taking place.

Most of the games had title screens that were generated from a LOT of keying in. The title screens that appeared from Mike Peace were done with the scroll mode keeping the cursor on the bottom of the screen. this allowed for editing up until dumping to tape. Because the screen image was saved with the data, it was the best way to do it. Mike was a good friend of mine then, and he shared a lot of his tips with me. He used the character generator described in the Arcadian and written by Mr. Skalas (I believe that's how you spell his name.). He would also use the multiplier feature to design his game boards. He would make a miniature of the maze he wanted and then blow it up 2 or 4 or 8 times. The best example of this is his Dungeons of  Dracula. All of the mazes in that game were done this way. Not only does this save space, it draws MUCH faster than box commands. You simply define a character, like in the DNA manual, and then when you call it up, you
 define the multiplier.
Mike White also used this technique throughout his Quadra game, and in his menu program with the rocket.

Mike Peace simply made a program that was extremely easy to use to do title screens and maze info. The castle in Castle of Horror and the mazes in Tomb Pirates  used the 2nd technique. (multiplying of a character)

Secrets of Pelucitar was done using the first technique. The screen never clears. some of it shifts, but never clears. This saves the programming space. You still have 1.8K to write the action part of the game.

It was just the opposite for me, I learned BASIC on the Bally and then I was able to learn BASICA on the IBM at work. I designed some crude graphics and print programs for my company to use during the DOS and CPM days. I also created some programs that did data manipulation of existing text files. This was extremely helpful in designing PCBs. The program I was using then could make text files of the database for editing purposes. Then I was using a program called Turbo BASIC. It was a compilable BASIC the could be compiled WITHOUT having any overhead like BRUN.
Now THAT was FUN!

This month, in issue 76 of the European magazine "Retro Gamer," there is a feature called "The 25 Best 8-Bit Arcade Conversions of All Time."  Number 25 on the list is actually an Astrocade game, which shocked me since this magazine NEVER mentions the Astrocade.  Here is what it says:

#25 - Space Fortress
Format: Bally Astrocade
     The Astrocade was an early peer of the Atari VCS, but was somewhat less successful.  However, it's tiny catalogue- barely 30 games- did contain an arcade port that knocked almost anything on the VCS into a cocked hat for accuracy and feel.  Weirdly, although Bally (via Midway) actually owned the arcade game in question (Space Zap), this isn't an official conversion, but it's identical in pretty much every way, and is probably the most insanely fast and frantic videogame of its era.  (If you can't get hold of an Astrocade- and you probably can't- Cosmic Zap on the Dragon 32 is almost as good.)

Comments?

Adam

Okay.  Here you go:

23) Kung Fu Master - Atari 2600
22) Jelly Monsters - Vic-20 (Port of Pac-Man)

18) Vanguard - Atari 5200

14) The Pit - Vic-20
13) Qix - Game Boy
12) S.T.U.N. Runner - Lynx

10) Popeye - NES
9) R-Type - Sega Master System
8) Buggy Boy - C64
7) Renegade - Spectrum 128
6) Space Invaders - Atari VCS, Hack Version
5) Planetoid - BBC Micro (Port of Defender)

a member of that site).

It's not surprising Retro Gamer doesn't mention the Astrocade much, since
it's a UK publication.
>>

I don't think that is the reason.  Retro Gamer talks about PLENTY of
obscure, never released in the UK, systems.  Retro Gamer has no trouble at
ALL covering NTSC systems.  I think they gloss over the Astrocade for two
reasons: 1) It has such a small library of games compared with other
systems, and 2) There is no proper way to emulate it fully (for instance,
you can't even play the included Gunfight properly).

>>
Was the Astrocade even distributed there [in the U.K.]?
>>

It wasn't released outside of the U.S.  Even certain regions of the U.S.
never saw a "heavy" release.  In areas around Ohio, where Astrocade was
located, and in California, the release seemed to have had strength.  This
is just personal observation thought, but I've noticed it over the years.

>>
[Retro Gamer] do an excellent job overall, though, and always have.
>>

Agreed.  If you've never read this magazine, then you're missing out!  A
12-issue subscription is quite pricey though, at about $150!  When I renewed
I was able to do it on the "cheap:" there was a special price of "only" $120
(I think that special is gone).  If you don't subscribe, you're probably
NEVER going to read it, because hardly any newstands carry it.  Try picking
up at least ONE issue though.  It's worth it.

8919:
I haven't posted anything for many months so after the moderator of this forum suggested I post a few comments regarding the "bally console" I can relate some experiences I had with Bally. In 1977 and after reading an advertisement in Popular Science I ordered a "Bally Home Library Computer" from JS&A. After some months of waiting, I finally received my BHLC in early 1978. It wasn't long after unpacking the unit and turning it on the Bally failed. Unhappy but still with high expectations, I sent it back and sometime later (I can't remember), I received another unit. I turned that one on but it wasn't an hour (maybe a couple) it failed in the same manner. So I received a 3rd one which finally "live" and we enjoyed for a couple of years. I should mention I did discover as many or most of you, the problem with the device was caused by its enemy, heat. After receiving the last Bally, I opened the case up, removed the top portion of the unit and "threw it
 away"! After removing the metal cover and with the power on I felt each chip and discovered a couple that gave off alot of heat. I glued a heat sink to each chip to further protect my "investment". I later found (at least my understanding) one of the delay in releasing the Bally console was the FCC approval in meeting emf/rf requirements.

 I later added the cassette tape interface and then the Bally Basic cartridge.  My kids played games and I fiddled with Basic.

A couple of years later I sold the unit (ouch)! I moved on to the Vic 20, C64 and then with PCs of which I currently have.I did expect but never did get any add-on devices such as the Zgrass unit.

No, I wasn't really kidding.  I'd like to figure out a bit more about the working of MESS and improve the Astrocade emulation.  As far as a RAM expansion goes, I've already gotten the equivalent of a Lil' WHITE RAM mostly running.  The files src/mess/drivers/astrocde.c sets up the address map for ROM and RAM.  I looked at some other drivers for examples, and managed to add extended RAM from 0x6000 to 0xdfff.  With this selected, I got Blue RAM BASIC and Vipersoft BASIC to start up, and did a simple test writing a value to extended memory and printing the result back out.  Before submitting anything, I'd really like to figure out how to choose different expansion sizes (i.e. 16K for a Viper System 1), and how to implement the switch to write protect RAM (temporarily treating it as ROM).  What would be more difficult, I imagine, is correctly implementing the Blue RAM expansions, since these use an extra chip.

I have one question someone here might be able to answer.  The extended RAM, at least typically, starts at 0x6000.  So a 4K expansion goes from 0x6000 to 0x6fff.  And, I believe, a 32K expansion goes from 0x6000 to 0xdfff.  But I've read that R&L Enterprises released an expansion that could go all the way up to 64K.  Adding this up in hexadecimal, I get 0x6000 to 0x15fff.  But if I try to go this high in MESS, nothing will run.  Is this memory range correct?

As you point out, MESS does still have the extremely annoying "Out of timers!" bug.  This mainly seems to affect AstroBASIC, and programs built off of it like the BASICarts.  I just asked about this on the forums at mess.org, and so far the information I've gotten is:

"Out of timers usually means something's allocating timers without disposing them. (Or it's using old-style anonymous timers, which hopefully not many things do now since it prevents supporting save states)."

Richard Degler put in his bug report:

"A cause of
this
is when the interrupt register $0E Hex is set to $18 for screen interrupts
PLUS
the undocumented unclipped light pen interrupts seen in the following bitmask
:

bit 0 - Light pen interrupt mode (see below)
bit 1 - Light pen (visible area) interrupt enable
bit 2 - Screen (at scanline set) interrupt mode
bit 3 - Screen (at scanline set) interrupt enable
bit 4 - Light pen (full screen) interrupt enable
and bits 5 to 7 - not used

where mode is 0 - to hold interrupt until Z-80 acknowledges it
or mode equal 1 - to cancel interrupt after next instruction."

Hopefully I'll learn more.  If anyone else feels like delving into the MESS source code, let me know.

Paul
8956:
The Lil' WHITE RAM can access as low as $5000. but that is a part of it's floating memory ability.(see instructions for a further explanation) R&L's 64Kram, pronounced "Sixty-four CRAM board" by them, can access from $0000 to $FFFF There are some safe guards the make accessing below 6K hard, but it cam be done.
The Blue Ram ONLY has a problem if you are using one of it's I/O functions. Unfortunately, it is always looking for the Blue Ram keyboard, which was a problem with some BASIC programs that were looking for the KP input. Every time you ask IF KP A=10, or something similar, the BRB1.1 would first check the keyBOARD then the keyPAD. I haven't used the MESS program, but I see how this could become a problem. Also if there was any input expected from the tape I/O. There also was a small RAM that could be accessed inside the INS8154. It's address was AFTER the main RAM and was only 128 bytes long. Mike Whites Quadra uses this ram, so if the MESS is not set up to access this area, then it won't work.
Ken

I think that there is some confusion here.  The 64K RAM Board only covers the address range from $0000-$FFFF.  As you can see, this overlaps with the Astrocade's memory map.  For normal use with the Astrocade, some of that RAM would NOT be usable.  In fact, it must be turned OFF.  That is, the area that would interfere with the System ROM on the expansion RAM board would not even need to be installed.  So, in effect, the board would really only be adding 56K of RAM.  The first 8K CAN be installed though (so it seems, anyway-- I don't know anyone that has done this), and this RAM would just bump out the ROM.  In this case, the Astrocade wouldn't boot unless the RAM was somehow filled with a machine language program (a game, an OS, or whatever can take control of the machine)

For an overview about this information, read page one of the 64K Ram Board manual, here:

file:///F:/Astrocade/Ballyalley/public_html/documentation/misc_hardware_docs/full_size/64k_ram_board.pdf

As a side note, I really did think that you were just pulling our leg about adding extra RAM support to MESS.  It's cool to see you working on it!

The first area of concern is the $0000 to $1FFF, the OBR (on-board ROM). This however is one way to check out the other system ROM programs, IE, White ROM, 3164, and 3159. The other thing is either to write your own BIOS or edit one or more on-board games.SYSEN and BUZOFF are used here.

2000-$3FFF is used for the cartridge slot and can be used by RAM to test out a new game, etc.

The other area not used is the $4000-$4FFF. This is screen RAM area. It theoretically could be used to have a faster RAM in there, but you have to make sure that the
SYSEN and BUZOFFare hooked right. BUT $5000-$FFFF is available for programming and Extended BASICS.

Ken

FOR A=!6000TO !7FFF:%(A)=A;NEXT A; FOR A= !8000TO !FFFF;%(A)=A;NEXT A
This approach works fine. If you are using machine language to do your loop stuff, it doesn't matter. I WILL go through because it doesn't see !8000 as a negative number.


I hope this clears up some mis-conceptions about the e=Extedned Memory systems

8977:
>>
I plan to write a few articles about the homebrew game design scene for 1UP and wanted to ask a few questions about Bally BASIC to anyone familiar with it
>>

Having read the comment that you should read the newsletter to get a better understanding of the BASIC scene (from the late 70's and early 80's), it really would take a LONG time, plus, since you don't know much about the Astrocade (I presume), much of the information wouldn't mean that much to you.  You're not looking to become a programmer, you just want a general idea of what the heck was going on with this strange-but-cool little game system.

>>
Summarize the experience of programming games in Bally BASIC.
>>

Programming in Bally BASIC is very-much like programming for ANY version of BASIC except that the programmer is limited to 1.8K.  The early games for the system were BASIC-only and were often quite crude (especially the ones published in the newsletters).  It wasn't until programmers started to mix the BASIC games with the on-board ROM's machine language subroutines that the better games began to trickle out.  This took awhile because it first required that the 8K ROM be understood.  At first, information about this was not available- people had to figure-it-out for themselves.

>>
What were the advantages that the language had over programming languages for other game consoles of the late 1970s and early 1980s?
>>

Lance made some observations here, but he failed to mention just how well-written the Bally BASIC manual is.  It's actually a tutorial of sorts.  Lance also mentions that you only needed a tape recorder.  Not true.  Bally BASIC, the BASIC that you seem to be asking about, required a tape interface that allowed you to save at 300-BAUD (meaning it took about four minutes to save 1.8K).  Later, AstroBASIC had a built-in tape interface that allowed loading and saving at 2000-BAUD (meaning a program could be loaded in about 20 seconds).

Unlike BASIC for the Atari 2600, you could actually use Bally BASIC for REAL programming.  Atari 2600 BASIC limited the programmer to only nine lines (I think).  I'm not sure what this corresponds to in RAM-size, but SMALL!  Also, BASIC for the 2600 didn't let you load or save.

The Odyssey 2 Programming cartridge wasn't really programming in machine language.  It was SIMULATED machine language.  Since the manual never SAYS this, many people don't understand that the language was interpreted (like BASIC).  Thus, you lose ALL advantages of assembly language speed.  Also, you can't load or save.

>>
What shortcomings did Bally BASIC have in comparison to dialects of BASIC for home computers?
>>

Many.  First and foremost would be limited RAM.  As I said, you only had 1.8K available for use (yes, the system had 4K total-- see Lance's FAQ about why you can't use it all).  Even if you upgraded your RAM (hardly something most people did), then Bally BASIC was STILL limited to 1.8K (though, later, people somehow were able to use expanded RAM for data).

Bally BASIC, unlike most BASICs of the time, was NOT based on Microsoft BASIC.  Bally BASIC is based on Tiny BASIC.  This makes sense from a technical standpoint, but it meant that one could not just pick-up a generic BASIC book and type in even a short program without usually making some changes.

PEEK and POKE was available for Bally BASIC, this was a cumbersome method for machine language of any sort.  Plus it would eat up the RAM available quite fast.

Most home computers had disc drives available for them.  The Astrocade never did.  Using BASIC with a disc drive is an entirely different experience from using BASIC with a tape drive.  This goes for ALL versions of BASIC.

In theory using any generic tape player for BASIC seems like a great idea.  You save money and don't have to buy another piece of equipment.  This usually worked-out fine if you were saving and loading tapes on your own computer.  In practice though, this usually meant that you had to fiddle around with the tape player's volume and tone settings in order to get tapes from another person's computer to run.  With the 300-BAUD tapes, this wasn't too much of a problem.  It wasn't until the newer AstroBASIC with 2000-BAUD ability was released that this became much of a problem.  This wasn't really a problem with BASIC as much as it was a problem with low-quality tape players themselves.  If there had been a quality, standard player, then this probably would not have occurred.  Then again, the whole POINT of Bally BASIC was to be inexpensive.  Making the owner buy extra hardware would have defeated the purpose of the inexpensive BASIC.

>>
What tools were necessary to program software in Bally BASIC?
>>

Lance did say everything that was needed (except for the tape interface, which I've already mentioned).  However, to get the most out of Bally BASIC, it really did require a subscription to a newsletter.  Since information for the Astrocade's version of BASIC wasn't generally available from any other source, these newsletters were a vital link for users to share information.  If these newsletters had never existed then I strongly believe that the commercial tapes never would have existed either.  Sure, there might have been the sharing of the tapes between friends who also owned Astrocades, but there would not have been the nationwide distribution that was available because of the newsletter.

>>
What were the limitations of the Astrocade hardware, and what did Bally BASIC users do to overcome them?
>>

The two limitations most noticeable are the keypad entry and the 1.8K of RAM.  Getting over the keypad entry doesn't take long.  In fact, it's quite easy to get used to.  Getting past the 1.8K of RAM is quite difficult.  I'm actually amazed at some of the games that were created in just 1.8K (especially the games that used extra color).

Some people designed and built their own keyboards, but this was rare.  Mostly people just lived with the keypad.  Like I said, it's not nearly as bad as it looks.

To get past the 1.8K of RAM people designed RAM expansion units.  These are quite rare now, but they were readily available in the early eighties.  In order to use that extra RAM new BASIC's were designed to take advantage of it.  These were first released on tape and then on cartridge.  Mostly, though, people DID NOT upgrade their Astrocade consoles.  They just made the best of what they had by learning how to get around RAM limitations by using ROM subroutines (when possible) and whatever else they could imagine.

>>
How did Bally BASIC games compare with official releases
>>

For the most part, Bally BASIC games compare poorly with cartridges.  Their are nearly 500 BASIC programs archived on Ballyalley.com (NOT all of them are games).  The earliest games are quite dull.  BASIC was just too slow for action games until people really started to learn tricks from the newsletters, which didn't really reach critical mass until AstroBASIC was released in 1981.  Once programmers began using the ROM routines, then the games began to run at a descent speed.  Trying some of those early pre-ROM routine BASIC "action" games is extremely DULL.  Still the programmers made the best of what they had available to them at the time.  There are quite a few games that are NOT action-oriented and they are fun.

>>
[what] shortcomings did Bally BASIC have next to games designed in assembly language?
>>

BASIC is MUCH slower than machine language.  Plus, machine language has the advantage of a larger palette.  Also, the machine language cartridges run from ROM, and up to 8K is available (though only the later games are that "large").  These advantages are enormous.  I can't think of ONE BASIC game that reaches what a cartridges can do (although some do try hard and come close-- though this is mostly because they have large parts written in ML).

>>
Which Bally BASIC games were outstanding, and what make them stand apart from the rest of the software written in the programming language?
>>

Search the message board and you'll find several lists for the best BASIC games.  This topic has come up several times before.  I think each time the lists end up being a little different, so check all of them

>>
How were Bally BASIC games distributed?
>>

Type-in programs were distributed through the newsletters, and, sometimes, sold by individuals (though this was rare).  I understand that some tapes were available through smaller retailers, but I don't know who.  For the most part though, if you didn't have a subscription to the newsletters, then you never would have heard about the tapes.

>>
How active is the Bally BASIC community today, and what new software has come from it in the past ten years?
>>

I'd say there are two parts to being active in the community.  There is the archival part of it.  This is quite active.  It has been going on for about ten years and I don't see an end in sight anytime soon.  Then there is the programming part.  Except for one full, EXCELLENT, game (called "War") most new programs have been demonstrations.  Since I know people will ask the status of the cartridge release of "War," it's on hold at the moment.  It shouldn't take long to tie up the loose ends, but I really have not had the time lately.

I believe that the reason that the Astrocade doesn't have more homebrew games is because the console is quite rare.  Also, when the console does pop up they tend to be broken.  When working consoles ARE bought, people do not usually know about the overheating trouble, so they end up with a dead console after not-too-long.  This is too bad, because the Astrocade has all of the documentation needed to make great games.  While it's obscure, the information needed to program the Astrocade is readily available.

Hopefully I've been able to fill-in some gaps here.  I'd like to see more information about programmers from the classic days.  It's kind of hard to ask the right questions though without knowing what to ask...

Also, whatever information that you DO use for your article, please be sure to give credit to the individual that gave it to you.  Nothing is written in a vacuum.

Lots of great responses so far...
Unfortunately, this is a very busy week for me (Apple's WWDC), otherwise I would try and find time to write more...

I was fascinated by the arcade when it came out. It had such... potential. The concept was great (that you could retask the commercial game chipset for home use, albeit with less resolution and colors...).

Understanding what made the Bally Arcade tick became an obsession for me. I reverse engineered the design and learned to program cartridges for it. But I get ahead of myself...

Digging into the machine, I used the Basic cartridge as a tool to examine the game system itself. I learned to write to registers to control music, graphics and controls. There were many folks digging into the mysteries of the Bally system, through collaboration, we figured lots of 'tricks' out and shared this with the other users through the Cursor and Arcadian newsletters.

I figured out how the music controls worked, and loved the three tone demo cart, I wanted to bring that feature to Basic programs. So I wrote the Three Tone Music Processor that George Moses programmed lots of music in. I transcribed a couple of songs, but got a lot more enjoyment out of figuring out the puzzle that was programming the Bally Arcade...

I explained how from Basic, one could 'poke' into memory values that could then be pointed to and executed as machine language instructions. Basically, I dictated the "Peek and Poke" information to Fred Cornet that he then transcribed into the "Peek and Poke Manual". And I wrote a few Basic programs that used this technique to offer interrupt driven graphics support (moving the graphics during the vertical interval) so that the graphics did not flicker. I think the program was called "Critter" because it moved a space invader like critter across the screen just like the cartridges did, but from Basic. And going further, I started playing with the color registers to see how many colors could be put on the screen at one time. With careful juggling, you could increase the number of colors, and if you wanted to have a lot of fun, you could even do a rainbow of colors!

So my passion with the Basic cartridge was seeing how far you could push the limits of the machine. How much you could extend the graphics, the music, the colors, etc.

Eventually, I learned enough to write a couple of cartridges myself (Treasure Cove and ICBM Attack).

It was a wonderful learning experience, teaching me the basics of computer fundamentals far better than the mundane classes I was taking in Electrical Engineering. I learned to code, then build hardware, and eventually I went on to designing ASICs. I started a few companies that built video boards for Apple computers, and eventually ended up working at Apple where I now head up the "Technology Advancement" group. And it all started with the Bally Arcade.

8984:
It sounds like you have custom chip problems. Usually the one underneath the keypad wires is the culprit. It is called the "Custom Data" chip. It SHOULD have a piece of aluminum glued on top for a heat sink. If it doesn't, chances are that it has burnt itself out. The biggest problem here is that there are NONE available worldwide, unless you get really lucky and find a working unit. I got lucky recently and had gotten a dead one, but I found out all 3 custom chips were still good. So I was able to use them in another unit that had blown out ones.
Here's how you check the bad ones out:

First take off the top cover. It comes off with the 5 screws on the bottom.

Next take the RF shield off completely These used to be there so they wouldn't interfere with the TV nearby that weren't connected to the Bally. It's the big piece of steel that covers at LEAST 1/2 of the unit. Leave it off! It trapped most of the heat generated by the custom chips.

Now remove the 4 screws that mount the PCB to the chassis. They are located in the corners.

Next, remove the chassis from the bottom plastic. Turn the chassis over and remove the 4 screws that hold the keypad/cassette assy on. Please be careful because the wires to the keypad can be fragile. This exposes the custom Data chip.

Now take the other units and start swapping out the 3 custom chips. They are the 3 in sockets with 40 pins each. Do NOT mix them up! The 86xy....115 is the custom I/O chip and should go into the socket closest to the hand control sockets. The ....116 chip goes in the middle position. This is called the Custom Address chip.

The 1st chip I would swap is the Data chip, as that usually gives the most problems.
The symptoms on the last unit sounds like it could be your Data chip.

Now for saving the one worker. REMOVE THE RF SHIELD. If you don't have small children around, remove the cover, too. the more free air that gets to the Data chip, the longer it should last. And Finally NEVER, NEVER, NEVER, dare I say NEVER operate the Bally / Astrocade on a rug, towel or any other cloth because it will restrict the air flow that is coming up from below. Always put it on a table (Without a cloth on it) or board, etc.

I hope you can get at least one more going. If you are still having problems, feel free to email me at:
kenzre@yahoo.com, and I will see if I can help you further.
Ken Lill

8994:
OK, now my 2 cents. Iv'e been an electronic engineering technician since the
late 70's (Time frame sound familiar to anyone?) I bought my first Bally from a
"Penny Saver" ad. It had the infamous "Space Invaders" game. The 300 baud
interface was home made by the guy I brought from.  I wish I had written down
his name. He probably worked for Midway, Bally or Dave Nutting. All of which
were local to Chicago, my then home town. I also got some CURSOR and ARCADIAN
newsletters from him. I quickly found out about the overheating problem and took
it to the local Bally repair shop. It was Rex TV on the south side of Chicago,
and got it repaired for a small fortune. The custom chips were going for $29-$39
dollars then, AND they were still available. I learned the putting the unit on a
rug, towel, or anything the blocked the lower vents caused the custom DATA chip
to overheat and kill itself. There was a "fix" in one of the newsletters, an
from what I gathered, it worked. (I sold on to Paul, a 3164 that I had gotten
with the fix and it was still working despite not having any heat sink.) The guy
at Rex finally asked me to tell him why these things were coming back after
about 1/2 hour of playing time. I told him to take 2 home and have his kids play
on while it was on their rug. Then when that quit, play the other on a coffee
table that had nothing on it but the Bally. I was going to be back the next week
to check up on his progress. When I went back he thanked me for the insight and
from then on he told all of his customers not to play the unit on the rug.

Fixes: a low height heat sink glued to the top of the DATA chip (the one under
the keypad wires) does wonders. It doesn't have to be fancy, a 1/8" thick 2-1/2"
by 1/2" piece of aluminum works fine.
2) a small fan, if you can deal with the noise, is the BEST solution.
3) Remove the heat shield. This always helps.

4) The laptop cooler system helps. It circulates a lot of air into the unit.
5) If you don't have any toddlers around, remove the top plastic.

I have been running my unit now for several years, including engineering the
Lil' WHITE Ram and the UltiMulti cart with it. I sometimes have left it on for
days with no ill effects.
I have an aluminum heat sink (glued on with one drop of Gorilla glue) and the
heat shield and top plastic removed.

As far as the current draw from the S-Video board, that board uses exactly the
same chip that the RF modulator uses, so the current draw is almost exactly the
same. Make sure of the clip connection, though.It will cause over-current if it
is too loose.

Please inform everyone that is using it to keep it off rugs!!!!!!

'Nough said
Ken Lill

8997:
it's me again. Just to say, from my experience, the lytics in the Bally are
pretty darn good. I have only had to replace one in the 20+ years I've been
working with them. It IS true, however that lytics dry out over the ages, but
the good thin id that ALL of the Bally's lytics are available @ Mouser, Jameco,
Allied, and dozens of other electronic component stores. As a matter of fact,
the only parts I've not been able to find directly are the 3 custom chips, the
power supply (although you can make up one with different components), the
keypad and the cassette contacts.Oh,yes, and the plastic parts. The chassis is
unavailable BUT, surprise guys, it is not necessary for the operation of the
unit. I ran mine for months without one.
You could replace all the lytics for about $15-20 if you know how to desolder
carefully, and resolder the new ones in. Be careful, some of the markings may be
different. A lot of old parts had the positive side marked whereas all of the
new ones have the negative side marked.
Ken

8998:
Yes, strangely, I usually have more problems with newer capacitors than older ones. I have a MSX1 here, built around 1986, and it seems to be working just fine. Amiga 500 computers also work perfectly to this date, but the newer Amiga 600 and 1200, which use earlier SMD capacitors, have an awful record of leaks and malfunctions. I subscribe an Amiga discussion group and, like the heat warning for Astrocade users, the first thing they say to the new users is to replace all capacitors in the newer Amiga models, because many circuit boards are simply destroyed by "silent" leaks.

Ronaldo

When I use my console for long periods, I totally remove the top of it.  Sometimes, if I'm programming it, I'll even have a small fan blowing air across the motherboard.  This works okay, but is probably overkill.  I know that installing low-profile heatsinks on the chips is an option, but I've never explored it.  Some people also mod their cases and put a small CPU fan in the area where the cartridges normally go.
